concepts.name: B-tree indexes and column order in composite indexes

questions.prompt: `messages` has a B-tree index on `(conversation_id, created_at)`. Which query can use it to scan only a small, contiguous part of the index?

choices.text: `WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day'`
`WHERE conversation_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at`
`WHERE role = 'user' AND created_at > '2026-01-01'`
`WHERE content LIKE '%refund%'`

questions.explanation: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then by the second within each value of the first, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name. Equality on the leading column (`conversation_id = 42`) narrows the scan to one contiguous range, already ordered by `created_at`. A condition only on `created_at` can't narrow the range, because matching entries are spread across every conversation. The last two don't involve the index's leading column at all.

questions.prompt: When does adding an index make things slower?

choices.text: When the indexed column is used to filter rows in a `WHERE` clause
When queries sort their results by the indexed column with `ORDER BY`
When the table already has a primary key on another column
On a write-heavy table, since each write must also update the index

questions.explanation: The PostgreSQL docs say that once an index exists the system must keep it in sync with the table, which adds overhead to every insert, update and delete, and that indexes seldom used by queries should be removed. Filtering and sorting on the indexed column are what an index is for. A primary key already has its own index, and adding another one is unrelated to slowness.

questions.prompt: You have a B-tree index on `(user_id, created_at)`. Explain how well it serves each of: `WHERE user_id = 7`; `WHERE user_id = 7 AND created_at > X`; `WHERE created_at > X`. Why?

model_answer.summary: The index is sorted by `user_id` first and `created_at` second, so it serves the first two queries well and the third poorly. Matching entries for `created_at` alone are scattered across every `user_id`.
key_points: The index is ordered by `user_id`, then by `created_at` within each `user_id`
`user_id = 7` uses the leading column, so the scan covers one contiguous range
`user_id = 7 AND created_at > X` is best: equality on the leading column plus a range on the next column narrows the scan further
`created_at > X` alone can't narrow the scanned range, so the planner often prefers a sequential scan or reads the whole index
If that query matters, add an index led by `created_at` (PostgreSQL 18's skip scan helps only when `user_id` has few distinct values)

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's rule is that equality constraints on leading columns, plus any inequality on the first column without an equality, limit the part of the index scanned. Conditions on later columns are checked in the index but don't shrink the range. Skip scan is new in PostgreSQL 18 and is chosen only when the leading column has few distinct values.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `EXPLAIN` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`?

choices.text: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the statement and reports real times and row counts
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` refreshes the table's statistics first, like the `ANALYZE` command
`EXPLAIN` runs the query, while `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` only estimates it
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows the same estimates, converted into milliseconds

questions.explanation: Plain `EXPLAIN` shows the planner's estimated plan and costs. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the statement and adds the actual time, rows and loops for each node. Because it really runs, an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` under `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` really changes data, so wrap it in `BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;`. It doesn't update statistics; that's the separate `ANALYZE` command.

questions.prompt: An `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` node shows `(actual time=0.003..0.003 rows=1 loops=10)`. Roughly how much time was spent in that node in total?

choices.text: 0.3 ms

questions.explanation: When a node runs more than once, as the inner side of a nested-loop join does, the reported time and rows are averages per loop. Multiply by `loops`: 0.003 ms × 10 = 0.03 ms. Cost numbers are in arbitrary planner units, but `actual time` is in milliseconds.

questions.prompt: You index `messages(role)`, where 60% of rows have `role = 'user'`. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on `WHERE role = 'user'` still shows a `Seq Scan`. Why?

choices.text: A new index can't be used until `VACUUM FULL` has run on the table
B-tree indexes can't be used for equality tests on text columns
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` always shows a sequential scan, whatever the real plan
Reading most of the table, a sequential scan is cheaper than index lookups

questions.explanation: The planner picks the plan with the lowest estimated cost. When a query needs a large fraction of the table, reading it front to back is cheaper than hopping between index entries and table pages. An index pays off for selective conditions that match a small share of rows. A new index is usable at once, and B-trees handle text equality fine.

questions.prompt: What is PostgreSQL's default transaction isolation level?

choices.text: Serializable
Repeatable Read
Read Committed
Read Uncommitted

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL's default is Read Committed: each statement sees data committed before that statement began. You can ask for Read Uncommitted, but in PostgreSQL it behaves exactly like Read Committed, so dirty reads never happen. Repeatable Read and Serializable must be requested explicitly.

questions.prompt: A transfer runs `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 1`, then a second `UPDATE` to credit account 2, inside `BEGIN`. The second statement fails and you run `ROLLBACK`. What is the state?

choices.text: Account 1 is debited, because its statement had already succeeded
Neither change persists: the transaction is all or nothing
Account 1 is debited until autovacuum cleans up the row
It depends on the isolation level of the transaction

questions.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction's statements take effect together or not at all. `ROLLBACK` cancels every change made since `BEGIN`, including the debit that succeeded. Isolation levels control what concurrent transactions see, not whether a rolled-back change survives.

questions.prompt: State in one line each what the four ACID properties mean. Then explain what your application must do when it runs transactions at PostgreSQL's Serializable level.

model_answer.summary: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability together make transactions safe under concurrency and crashes. At Serializable, PostgreSQL may abort a transaction with a serialization failure, and the application must retry it.
key_points: Atomicity: all of a transaction's operations happen, or none do
Consistency: committed data always satisfies the database's integrity constraints
Isolation: a transaction's changes aren't visible to concurrent transactions before it commits
Durability: once committed, changes survive a crash or power failure
At Serializable, transactions can fail with a serialization error, so the app must be ready to retry the whole transaction

questions.explanation: These definitions follow the PostgreSQL glossary. Serializable prevents every anomaly in the isolation table, and it does so by aborting one of the transactions that conflict. The docs state that applications using this level must be prepared to retry.

questions.prompt: An endpoint loads 50 conversations with one query, then loops over them and runs one query per conversation to fetch its messages. How many queries is that?
questions.explanation: That's the N+1 pattern: 1 query for the parent rows plus N = 50 queries for their children. Each is a separate round trip, so the endpoint gets slower as the list grows. Loading all the messages in one extra query (`WHERE conversation_id IN (...)`) brings it down to 2, and a join to 1.

questions.prompt: Explain the N+1 query problem, how it usually creeps into code that uses an ORM, and two ways to fix it.

model_answer.summary: N+1 is one query for a list of parents plus one more query per parent for its related rows. ORMs cause it through lazy loading; fix it by loading the related rows eagerly, with a join or with one batched `IN` query.
key_points: One query loads N parent rows, then N more queries load each parent's related rows
Cost grows with N because each query is a separate round trip to the database
ORM lazy loading hides it: touching `conversation.messages` in a loop silently runs a query each time
Fix 1: a JOIN that loads parents and children in one query (SQLAlchemy `joinedload`)
Fix 2: a second query fetching all children with `WHERE parent_id IN (...)` (SQLAlchemy `selectinload`), for 2 queries in total

questions.explanation: The SQLAlchemy docs describe N+1 as a side effect of lazy loading, solved by eager loading. SQLModel sits on SQLAlchemy, so the same loader options apply, and `raiseload` can turn an accidental lazy load into an error during tests.
